Reviewer #1:

The authors have improved the clarity of the manuscript substantially. My prior concerns have been adequately addressed. In addition to the specific comments below I would ask for additions/clarifications on three subjects.

I) First, on the path of the computation: Figure 1 is clearly the axis for most readers to understand the spike sorting process. Having carefully read the revised text as well as the original, I am still not sure how the original clustering is done. For the step of template collection, the text seems to imply that there are N clustering steps for the N electrodes. If true, one expects that each neuron would be detected on 3-8 electrodes and thus there are 3-8 times more clusters than neurons at least. The content of 1 C implies that these very many clusters are reduced to a template with 57 site "snipets" that make up the template. However, the example of 1C is centered on a maximum amplitude transient. How those maximum amplitude "centers" for templates are found is not clear to me, nor is how the expected variation around that center accommodated. Perhaps it does not need to be, since the template field is large so even is the maximum amplitude site for a given spike is off center, there is still ample information to cluster. A clear delineation of this template creation and use process would be useful, especially if it can be done pictorially as well as mathematically. How are all these redundant units merged?

II) While reading the Materials and methods section especially, but also reading the manuscript, I was constantly looking back through the text for the definition of variables and symbols. Would it be possible for the authors to make a variable definition table so that a reader can have access in one place to be reminded of variable definition for all variables in the paper?

III) The use of BEER is much better explained, but it would be useful to discuss when this assumption of elliptical boundaries is unlikely true, such as bursting cells or electrode-tissue drift.

Reviewer #3:

Let me begin by stating that it is very worthwhile to have a publication that describes SpyKING CIRCUS, since it is one of a handful of tools aimed at the automated analysis of multielectrode data.

Some comments follow:

1) This paper needs significant proofreading/editing to make it more readable.

As an example, the second sentence in the second section (Results) is:

“First, spikes are being detected as threshold crossings (Figure 1A) and isolated the extracellular waveforms for a number of randomly chosen spike times.”

I know what the authors intend, but it is garbled.

2) The Results section contains a description of the algorithm. Is that the format eLife requires? It would be clearer to have sections on the Algorithm, experimental results, validation experiments, etc.

3) A distinguishing feature of the method is the ability to resolve overlapping spikes in large systems in a reasonably automatic fashion and makes this an interesting contribution.

4) Other groups have used artificial template/spike insertion as a way to validate the algorithm and some reference could be given (e.g. Rossant 2016, Chung 2017).

5) The authors use cross-correlograms in order to help automate the merging process. It should be noted that, as a side effect, one can no longer use cross-correlograms as a validation metric.

6) Equation 1 is very confusing. The authors should explain the double sum notation (why index over events and units)? I'm sure they have something in mind but I don't know what it is.

results.result: The authors developed SpyKING CIRCUS, a spike sorting algorithm combining density-based clustering and template matching. The algorithm detects spikes as threshold crossings, divides them into groups by electrode position, performs parallelized clustering to extract templates (each with two waveform components), and uses greedy template matching to identify all spike times.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C35, C41-C64 describe the algorithm design and are internally consistent. The methodology is clearly described with specific implementation details (e.g., C50: maximum 10 clusters per electrode, C47: clustering inspired by Rodriguez & Laio 2014). The two-step approach (clustering then template matching) is well-justified as addressing limitations of clustering-only methods (C60-C62).

results.result: The algorithm achieved near-optimal performance on ground truth data from simultaneous extracellular and loose patch recordings. Performance was close to a nonlinear classifier (BEER) benchmark for both in vitro (4.8% vs 2.7% error for large spikes) and in vivo (14.8% vs 13.9% error) recordings, with error rates correlating with spike amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C65-C76 provide quantitative validation with appropriate ground truth data and statistical support (r=0.89, p<10⁻⁵ for in vitro; r=0.92, p<10⁻⁵ for in vivo). The comparison to BEER classifier provides a reasonable benchmark. However, the in vivo validation is limited (only 2 neurons with low error rates, C73-C74), and the BEER metric has acknowledged limitations (C156-C158).

results.result: The algorithm scales linearly to thousands of electrodes through parallelization, achieving real-time processing (1 hr data in 1 hr with 9 CPU cores for 252 electrodes) and maintaining <5% error rate on hybrid datasets with up to 4225 electrodes, independent of firing rate or electrode count.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C84-C96, C101-C102 demonstrate scalability with quantitative evidence from hybrid datasets. Linear scaling with electrodes (C90), templates (C91), and data length (C87) is shown. Performance consistency across different scales (C93, C96) is well-documented. The parallelization strategy is clearly described (C85-C86) and validated experimentally (C88-C89).

results.result: SpyKING CIRCUS achieved similar accuracy to Kilosort (4.4% vs 4.2% error) but with much lower memory footprint, enabling processing of thousands of electrodes. Kilosort was faster with GPU (4× speedup) but only marginally faster without GPU (1.5×) and cannot scale beyond hundreds of electrodes due to memory constraints (32 GB RAM for 500 neurons).
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C83 provide direct quantitative comparison with Kilosort. The performance similarity (C77) and speed/memory trade-offs (C78-C82) are clearly documented. The claim that Kilosort cannot scale to thousands of electrodes (C83) is supported by the memory usage data (C81). However, the comparison is limited to a single competing algorithm.

results.result: The template matching algorithm correctly resolves overlapping spikes, enabling unbiased estimation of pairwise correlations between neurons. The method recovered injected correlations with no underestimation, even for thousands of electrodes.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C100 address a critical challenge in spike sorting. The validation using hybrid datasets with controlled correlations (C98) provides direct evidence. The logical chain from overlapping spike detection to unbiased correlation estimation (C97, C99, C100) is sound and supported by Figure 3G data.

results.result: The authors developed an automated merging tool to combine split units from the same cell, using template similarity and cross-correlogram dip analysis. The automated method achieved error rates close to ground-truth-guided merging, with performance robust to parameter choices, enabling fully automated spike sorting.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C112 describe the automated merging solution with clear methodology (C107-C109) and validation (C110-C111). The approach addresses a practical bottleneck in large-scale sorting (C105). However, C113 notes an important limitation: cross-correlograms can no longer be used as an independent validation metric since they're used in the merging process itself.

results.result: Large-scale spike sorting for thousands of electrodes remains largely unresolved. Existing algorithms have limitations: they don't account for multi-electrode spike detection, don't scale computationally, and haven't been validated on real ground truth data. Available ground truth data are rare and often inadequate (simplified in vitro conditions or distant electrodes in vivo), and simulations may not capture biological variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C34 establish the problem context through citations to prior work. The characterization of existing limitations (C20-C23) and ground truth data scarcity (C24-C28) is well-supported. The critique of simulation-based validation (C29-C32) identifies real concerns about biological realism. This provides strong motivation for the presented work.

results.result: Classical clustering-based spike sorting approaches face three major problems for large-scale recordings: difficulty automating cluster border detection, computational challenges with thousands of electrodes, and missing overlapping spikes. The presented method addresses these by parallelizing clustering, only inferring cluster centroids (not borders), and using template matching to resolve overlaps. Previous template matching approaches lacked ground truth validation and couldn't model spike shape variation.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C135 provide context for the methodological choices through comparison with prior approaches. The three problems with classical methods (C122-C124) are well-established in the field. The advantages of the presented approach (C126-C128) logically address these limitations. The comparison with prior template matching work (C129-C132) is supported by citations and identifies specific improvements.

results.result: The method enables spike sorting from large-scale recordings in vitro and in vivo. The algorithm has been tested on synthetic datasets, validated by external groups, used by other researchers, and is available as open-source software with public ground truth data for benchmarking future methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C119, C39-C40 summarize the broader impact and availability of the work. External validation (C116) and adoption by other groups (C117) provide independent support. results.result: Manual curation time is a common bottleneck for large-scale spike sorting. The automated merging tool speeds up curation and reduces sensitivity to human errors and decision variability, though experiment-specific variables may sometimes require consideration.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C139 identify a practical problem (C136) and describe benefits of the solution (C137-C138). The caveat in C139 appropriately acknowledges limitations. These claims are logical inferences from the automated merging results rather than directly measured outcomes.

results.result: The method can run in real-time with sufficient computing power, paving the way for online spike sorting needed for brain-machine interfaces and closed-loop experiments. Online implementation would require processing data on-the-fly and adapting templates over time.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C143 discuss future potential for online processing. While C140 is supported by the parallelization results (C89), claims C141-C143 are speculative about future applications and requirements. The real-time capability is demonstrated, but actual online implementation and template adaptation have not been tested.

results.result: Recent technological developments in multielectrode arrays enable recording from hundreds to thousands of densely packed electrodes, providing high spatial resolution access to large neural ensembles. This creates a need for novel spike sorting methods, as each electrode receives activity from many neurons and spikes from single neurons appear on multiple electrodes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C9-C17 establish the technological and scientific context through citations to prior work. These are well-established facts in the field (C1, C11-C13) and logical consequences of the technology (C14-C15). The motivation for new methods (C2, C10) follows logically from the technological capabilities and neuroscience needs.

results.result: The algorithm performs close to optimal across a broad range of signal-to-noise ratios in vitro and in vivo, offering a fast and accurate generic solution for spike sorting up to thousands of electrodes, available as multi-platform parallelizable software.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C8, C37-C38, C76 are high-level summary statements supported by the detailed results in other claim groups. These represent valid conclusions from the validation studies (ground truth and hybrid datasets) and scalability tests. The characterization as 'generic solution' (C8, C37) is justified by testing across multiple conditions.

results.result: The experimental methods included in vitro retinal recordings (252 or 4225 electrodes, 20 kHz sampling) from rat/mouse and in vivo cortical recordings (32-128 electrodes, 30 kHz) from rat. Data preprocessing involved Butterworth filtering, spatial whitening, and PCA dimensionality reduction. The BEER classifier benchmark has limitations (not a strict lower bound, assumes ellipsoidal boundaries) but is an accepted standard. The software is implemented in Python with MPI for parallelization.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C162 describe experimental and computational methods. These are straightforward methodological descriptions with appropriate detail. The acknowledgment of BEER limitations (C156-C158) while justifying its use as an accepted benchmark (C159) shows appropriate critical awareness. The methods are sufficiently detailed for reproducibility.

results.result: Many spike sorting methods assume clustering alone solves the problem, but this neglects overlapping spikes. When nearby cells spike synchronously, their waveforms superimpose, distorting feature estimation and causing overlapping spikes to appear far from their respective clusters where they are missed by clustering-only approaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C55 identify a key limitation of clustering-only approaches with clear logical reasoning. The superposition of waveforms (C53) and resulting feature distortion (C54-C55) are well-established phenomena in spike sorting, supported by citation (C53) and illustrated in Figure 1C. This provides strong justification for the template matching step.
